title: The Opera Game

moves: e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 d6 Nf3 g6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb3 Bg7 Qe2 Nc6 O-O O-O h3 a5 a4 dxe5 dxe5 Nd4 Nxd4 Qxd4 Re1 e6 Nd2 Nd5 Nf3 Qc5 Qe4 Qb4 Bc4 Nb6 b3 Nxc4 bxc4 Re8 Rd1 Qc5 Qh4 b6 Be3 Qc6 Bh6 Bh8 Rd8 Bb7 Rad1 Bg7 R8d7 Rf8 Bxg7 Kxg7 R1d4 Rae8 Qf6+ Kg8 h4 h5 Kh2 Rc8 Kg3 Rce8 Kf4 Bc8 Kg5

annotations.text: Tilburg, 1991. England's Nigel Short plays Dutch star Jan Timman. This game is remembered for one of the most surprising plans in chess history.
**Alekhine's Defence**: Black invites White's pawns forward, hoping they become targets later.
White keeps a pawn on e5. It takes away the f6 and d6 squares from Black's pieces and cramps Black's position.
Black's queen is centralised on d4, but White will soon chase it around with gain of time.
**21.Qh4** swings White's queen to the kingside, next to Black's king.
**23.Bh6** offers to trade Black's best defender, the bishop on g7, which guards the dark squares around the king.
Timman avoids the trade with **23...Bh8**, but on h8 the bishop is very passive.
**24.Rd8** invades with the rook, pinning Black's pieces to the back rank.
The rook settles on d7, the seventh rank, hitting c7 and f7. Black is being squeezed.
White's queen sits on f6, right next to Black's king. One more attacker on g7 or h8 would be checkmate. But which piece can get there?
Black is holding for now: no white piece can reach g7 or h8. Black's pieces are frozen, though, and Timman can only shuffle.
**31.Kh2!** The answer is the king! Black has no way to attack it, so White's king can walk up the board and help with the mate.

annotations.text: Step two: **32.Kg3**. Timman's pieces can only shuffle back and forth.
**33.Kf4** climbs on, using the dark squares that Black can no longer defend.
Timman resigned. The plan is **Kh6**, and then **Qg7** is checkmate. Lesson: if the opponent has no way to attack it, your king can be a strong attacking piece.
annotations.label: Black resigns

questions.prompt: White to play. Black's bishop on g7 protects the dark squares around the king. What would you do?
questions.hint: Remove the defender.
questions.explanation: **27.Bxg7** trades off Black's best defender. Now the dark squares around the black king are weak, and White's queen can move in.

questions.prompt: White to play. Without its bishop, the black king has holes all around it. Where does the queen belong?
questions.hint: Find a check on a dark square.
questions.explanation: **29.Qf6+** puts the queen right next to the king. From f6 it eyes g7 and h8, and Black will have to defend them forever.

questions.prompt: White to play. Your king has already reached f4. What is the next step of the walk?
questions.hint: Keep marching towards h6.
questions.explanation: **34.Kg5!** The king heads for h6, where it will protect the queen on g7 for checkmate. Black cannot stop it.

title: The Immortal Zugzwang Game
summary: Nimzowitsch slowly squeezes White until every one of his pieces is tied up. At the end White has plenty of legal moves but no good ones: a rare zugzwang in the middle of the game, with almost all the pieces still on the board.

4...Bb7. The Queen's Indian Defence: Black's bishop watches the long diagonal and the key e4 square.
8.Ne5. White's knight jumps forward and opens the bishop on g2 towards Black's queenside.
11...b5. Black grabs space on the queenside and takes the c4 square away from White's pieces.
15...Nh5. The knight goes to the edge with a purpose: it hits the bishop on f4 and prepares ...f5.
16...f5. Black takes firm control of e4. White's pieces are starting to run out of good squares.
18.Nb1. The knight has to go all the way back to its starting square. White is getting cramped.

annotations.text: 18...Bb5. The bishop finds a great diagonal, eyeing e2 and the light squares in White's camp.
20.e4. White finally tries to break free. With the e-pawn gone from e2, his queen on d1 now attacks the knight on h5.

24...Bd3. The bishop lands on d3 and cuts White's position in two. Black's pieces dominate the whole board.

annotations.text: 25...h6!! A quiet pawn move that also gives Black's king an escape square. Now White is in **zugzwang**: he has many legal moves, but every one of them loses material or lets Black's attack crash through. Sämisch resigned.

title: Adams vs Torre: The Back-Rank Dance
summary: White offers his queen again and again, and Black can never take it because his own back rank is too weak. The most famous lesson ever on back-rank weakness and deflection: a piece that has to guard something can be chased until it breaks.

Black's knight attacked White's queen on d4, so 5.Bb5 pins it to Black's king.

16.Rae1: White's rooks are doubled on the open e-file, staring at the rook on e8.

annotations.text: 17.Bxf6 removes the knight. Now Black's back rank has a problem: his king has no escape square, and only the queen keeps e8 safe.

annotations.text: 19.Qc4! Again the queen is offered. Taking it allows Rxe8+ and mate, so Black's queen must move again.

questions.explanation: 22.Re4! attacks the queen. Taking the rook would just lose the queen to 23.Rxe4, so the queen must find another square that still guards e8, and only b5 is left.

title: Fischer vs Fine: Evans Gambit
summary: In a friendly game, Fischer gives away pawns to get his pieces out fast, and a former world-class grandmaster is lost in 17 moves. A perfect lesson in why development and king safety matter more than grabbing pawns.
moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O dxc3 Qb3 Qe7 Nxc3 Nf6 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nxe5 Qxe5 Bb2 Qg5 h4 Qxh4 Bxg7 Rg8 Rfe1+ Kd8 Qg3

annotations.text: New York, 1963. In a friendly game, Fischer meets Reuben Fine, a former world-class grandmaster. Fischer picks an old, swashbuckling opening to show that **fast development** can beat extra pawns.
Both bishops point at the weakest squares in each camp: f7 and f2. This is the Italian Game.
4.b4!? is the **Evans Gambit**. White gives a pawn to gain time: when Black takes it, White builds a big centre with c3 and d4, attacking as he goes.

annotations.text: 6.d4 opens lines. Fischer isn't worried about pawns; he wants his pieces out fast.

8.Qb3 lines up the queen and bishop against f7, the weakest point next to Black's king.
White wins one pawn back and brings out another piece. Look at the difference: almost all of White's pieces are in play, while Black has only three out and his king is still in the centre.
10.Nd5 jumps forward and hits the queen on e7. Almost every White move comes with a threat.
Black tries to trade pieces. Trading is a good way to defend, but Black's king is still stuck in the middle.

The king slips to d8, but it is surrounded by its own pieces and has no safe home.

questions.explanation: 17.Qg3! sets up 18.Bf6+, which checks the king and attacks the queen on h4 at the same time. If Black takes the queen, 18.Bf6 is checkmate because the rook on e1 covers e8 and e7.

title: Deep Blue wins the match
event: Deep Blue vs Kasparov rematch, New York
summary: The deciding game of the 1997 rematch. Kasparov slips in the opening, Deep Blue sacrifices a knight to keep his king stuck in the centre, and the world champion resigns after only 19 moves. It was the first time a computer won a match against a reigning world champion.

**4...Nd7** prepares **...Ngf6**, so that if White trades knights Black can take back with the other knight and keep a healthy pawn structure.
**5.Ng5** is a sharp idea: the knight eyes f7 and e6, two sensitive squares near Black's king.

Deep Blue doesn't rush. It castles first, bringing the rook closer to the e-file where Black's king will be stuck.

**16.Qd3** brings the queen into the attack. All of White's pieces are active; half of Black's are not.
Material is roughly level again, but Black's king is bare and his pieces are tangled. White's attack keeps going.

**19.c4** opens even more lines towards Black's king, and Kasparov resigned. It was the first match win by a computer over a world champion. Lesson: know your opening move orders, and a king stuck in the centre is a big target.
annotations.label: Kasparov resigns

title: Capablanca's Back-Rank Bolt

annotations.text: Amsterdam, 1889. A 20-year-old Emanuel Lasker, who would later be world champion for 27 years, plays White against Johann Bauer. Watch where White's two bishops are pointing.
1.f4. Bird's Opening: White grabs control of the e5 square with a pawn instead of the usual 1.e4 or 1.d4.
5.Bd3. Both bishops are now aimed at Black's kingside: one at h7, the other along the long diagonal.
8...O-O. Black castles right into the line of fire of those two bishops.
10.Ng3. The knight heads towards h5, ready to join the attack on Black's king.
12.Bxe5. After the trade, the bishop sits on e5 and stares at g7. Only the knight on f6 holds Black's position together.
13...a6? Black plans a queenside push and forgets about his king. This slow move gives Lasker the time he needs.
annotations.label: A slow move

annotations.text: 14.Nh5! White offers the knight to lure away the knight on f6, the key defender of h7.
15...Kxh7. The first bishop is gone, but now 16.Qxh5+ wins back the knight with check and the queen joins the attack.
annotations.label: First bishop sacrifice

annotations.text: 17...Kxg7. Both bishops have been given up, but Black's king has lost all of its pawn shelter.
annotations.label: Second bishop!

annotations.text: 19...e5. The only defence. This move opens the sixth rank so Black's queen can block a check on h6.
21.Rxh6+. White wins Black's queen. Count it up: Lasker gave two bishops and a rook, and got back a knight, the queen and two pawns.
annotations.label: Queen won

annotations.text: 23.Qxb7. The bishop falls. Material is now roughly level, but Black's king is bare and White's queen and rook keep pressing.
27.fxe5. White opens the f-file for his rook, pointing straight at Black's king on f8.
28.e6. The extra pawn marches forward, cramping Black and loosening the defence around his king even more.
30.Rxf6+! The rook crashes through. After 30...Bxf6 31.Qxf6+ the queen chases the king and aims at the loose rook on b7.
34.Qxb7. The rook on b7 falls with the help of the queen's checks. White now has a queen against a rook: a winning ending.
38.Qxd3. Black's last hope, the passed d-pawn, is gone and Bauer resigned. Sacrificing on h7 and g7 is now known as **Lasker's combination**. Watch out when both enemy bishops point at your king!

questions.prompt: White to play. Black just took your knight on h5. Both of your bishops point at Black's king. What's the bold follow-up?

questions.explanation: 15.Bxh7+! The bishop rips away the h7 pawn with check. After 15...Kxh7 16.Qxh5+ White wins back the knight with check, and Black's king is exposed.

questions.hint: A rook can travel along the third rank.
questions.explanation: 19.Rf3! The rook swings over to h3 for a deadly check. Black's only defence is 19...e5 20.Rh3+ Qh6, and then White wins the queen.

questions.prompt: White to play. Your attack has won back the material. Now find a move that attacks two black pieces at once!
questions.hint: Look at the bishops on e7 and b7.
questions.explanation: 22.Qd7! A double attack: the queen hits both the bishop on e7 and the bishop on b7. Black can only save one of them.

title: Tal vs Smyslov: The Magician
summary: Mikhail Tal, the Magician from Riga, lets a bishop go, throws his pieces at a former world champion's king and finishes with a queen sacrifice. It shows how activity and threats can be worth more than material.

title: Légal's Mate
summary: A seven-move miniature that gave its name to a classic trap. White gives up the queen, and three minor pieces deliver mate. The lesson: a pin is only a pin if breaking it really loses something, and grabbing the queen without looking can be fatal.
moves: e4 e5 Bc4 d6 Nf3 Bg4 Nc3 g6 Nxe5 Bxd1 Bxf7+ Ke7 Nd5#

annotations.text: Paris, around 1750, at the famous Café de la Régence. Légal, one of the best players of his day, sets a trap that still catches players today.
1.e4 grabs the centre and opens lines for the queen and the bishop.
1...e5 Black answers in kind, claiming a share of the centre.
2.Bc4 aims the bishop at f7, the weakest point in Black's camp, guarded only by the king.
2...d6 protects e5 and opens a path for the c8 bishop.
3.Nf3 develops a knight and attacks the e5 pawn.
3...Bg4 pins the knight to the White queen: if the knight moves, the queen on d1 is exposed.
annotations.label: The pin

annotations.text: 4.Nc3 develops another piece and quietly adds an attacker to the d5 square.
4...g6? A slow move. Black should be developing pieces, and it does nothing about White's hidden trick on e5.
5...Bxd1? Black takes the queen without looking at what White threatens. It's the losing move.
annotations.label: Taking the bait

annotations.text: 6.Bxf7+ The bishop strikes f7 with check, protected by the knight on e5. The king has only one square: e7.
6...Ke7 was the only move. Now look at which squares around the king are still free.
7.Nd5# Checkmate with three minor pieces! Black is a queen up but lost the game. **Before grabbing material, always ask what your opponent threatens.**
annotations.label: Checkmate!

questions.prompt: White to play. Your knight on f3 is pinned to the queen. Can you break the pin anyway?
questions.hint: Is losing the queen really a problem if you have something stronger ready?
questions.explanation: 5.Nxe5! If Black takes the queen with 5...Bxd1, White mates with 6.Bxf7+ and 7.Nd5#. If instead 5...dxe5, then 6.Qxg4 and White is a pawn up.

questions.hint: Your knight on c3 has a jump that gives check.
questions.explanation: 7.Nd5# The knight checks from d5, and the bishop and other knight cover every escape square.

title: Carlsen at 13

summary: A 13-year-old Magnus Carlsen sacrifices a knight, a bishop and a rook to tear open the black king and finishes with a beautiful checkmate. The game made the chess world notice the future world champion and shows how a pawn on h5 can become the spearhead of an attack.

annotations.text: Wijk aan Zee, January 2004. Thirteen-year-old Magnus Carlsen plays Dutch grandmaster Sipke Ernst. This attack made the chess world take notice. Carlsen became world champion in 2013.
The **Caro-Kann**: Black supports **...d5** with the c-pawn, a solid way to fight for the centre.
**4...Bf5** brings the light-squared bishop out before playing **...e6**, so it won't get locked in.
**6.h4** pushes the h-pawn to chase the bishop and grab space on the kingside.
The pawn reaches h5. Remember it: it will play a starring role later on.
Carlsen castles long. With the kings on opposite sides, both players can throw pawns and pieces at the other king.
Ernst castles short, right in front of White's h5-pawn. That pawn already controls g6.
**16.Ne5** puts the knight on a strong central square, eyeing f7 and g6.
Ernst hits back in the centre with **17...c5**. But White's pieces are aimed at the black king. Is there a way to break in?
Ernst takes the knight. Now the e6-pawn has lost its friend on f7, and White's h5-pawn can recapture on g6.

**25.Rd3!** The last rook swings over towards the g-file to join the attack.
